worksheet.title: The Missing Block
worksheet.subtitle: Add the block that's missing
worksheet.learning_goal: I can fix a program by adding a missing block.

parts.title: Not far enough!
parts.text: Sometimes a program is MISSING a block, so Bit falls short and never reaches the target. Run the code, see how far short it is, and add the missing block in the empty space.

parts.title: Program 1 — target is 4
parts.note: Write the missing block in the empty space.

parts.title: Run it — too short
parts.prompt: Run Program 1 from 1 (forward 2). What number does Bit land on? How many more does it need to reach 4?

parts.title: Add the missing block
parts.prompt: Write the block that gets Bit from where it stopped to 4. Run the fixed code — what number now?

parts.title: Program 2 — target is 1
parts.note: Write the missing block in the empty space.

parts.title: You try — add to fix
parts.prompt: Run Program 2 from 4 (back 1). It lands on 3, not 1. Write the missing block so Bit reaches 1. What block did you add, and where does Bit land?

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: If a program falls short, it may be missing a block. Add the step that finishes the job so Bit lands right on the target.

parts.title: Goal
parts.text: Students fix a bug where a program falls short of the target because a block is missing; they add the missing step and run again to confirm. Altering existing code by adding a step (and writing that step) covers C3.2 and a focused piece of C3.1.

parts.title: Ontario curriculum (Grade 1 — C3 Coding)
text: C3.1 — solve problems and create computational representations of mathematical situations by writing and executing code, including code that involves sequential events.
C3.2 — read and alter existing code, including code that involves sequential events, and describe how changes to the code affect the outcomes.

parts.title: Materials
parts.text: The printed worksheet and a pencil. Optional: a floor number path 0-5 so students see Bit stop short and count the steps left to the target.

parts.title: Run it (about 20 min)
text: 1. I DO: run Program 1 — 'start 1, forward 2 to 3. The target is 4 — Bit is one short. We need one more forward.'
2. WE DO: Exercise 1 — Bit lands on 3, one short. Exercise 2 — add 'forward 1'; the program reaches 4.
3. YOU DO: Exercise 3 — Program 2 lands on 3, two too high for target 1; add 'back 2' so 3 → 1.
4. Connect: 'Falling short can mean a missing block — add the step that finishes the job.'

parts.title: Answer key (modelled by the run-gate)
text: Ex 1 — Program 1: 1 → forward 2 → 3. Bit is on 3, one short of 4.
Ex 2 — add 'forward 1': 1 → 3 → 4. Bit reaches the target, 4.
Ex 3 — Program 2: 4 → back 1 → 3. Add 'back 2': 3 → 1. Bit reaches the target, 1. (Two 'back 1' blocks also work.)

parts.title: Watch for & differentiate
text: Common slip: adding a block that overshoots — have students count the gap from where Bit stopped to the target, then add a step of that size.
Simplify: do Program 1 only (one forward short).
Extend: ask for a different way to fix Program 2 (e.g. two 'back 1' blocks) and test it.
Success indicator: the child adds 'forward 1' to reach 4 and a back block (back 2, or two back 1s) to reach 1.
